title: Good faith in performance
summary: Good faith limits the way a party performs or exercises rights under an existing contract. Its content depends on the bargain, the governing law, and the particular choice or conduct at issue.
notes:
Dalton required the testing service to carry out its promised review process meaningfully; it did not authorize a court to replace the service’s assessment with its own. Market Street examines whether a party deliberately exploited the other’s oversight of a contractual procedure. Bloor asks whether the brewer made the effort required by an express best-efforts clause despite its own commercial pressures.

The casebook also presents different explanations of good faith, including excluding bad-faith conduct and limiting recapture of opportunities surrendered in the bargain. Those theoretical accounts help ask what the alleged opportunism consists of, but the legal duty still needs to be tied to the agreement. Northwest and Ng Giap show important limits, including preemption and reluctance to imply a broad obligation inconsistent with express rights.

Good faith is not an independent permission to impose whatever outcome seems fair, and it does not always require sacrificing all self-interest. Ask which benefit or procedure was promised, how the party’s conduct affected it, and what the governing authority actually requires.
